JSON: A way of converting an object into a string so it can be stored or sent to other machines, then parsed back to the same object (slide 6). See [Four review programs: block scope, hoisting and the event queue](#/comp4537-l3/review-predicts).
web storage|localStorage|sessionStorage: Browser storage of string key/value pairs, shared by pages of the same origin in the same browser; local storage is permanent, session storage expires (slide 7). See [Four review programs: block scope, hoisting and the event queue](#/comp4537-l3/review-predicts).
function-scoped: How var declares a variable: visible in the whole function (or the whole script), not just its block (slide 10). See [Four review programs: block scope, hoisting and the event queue](#/comp4537-l3/review-predicts).
block-scoped: How let and const declare a variable: visible only inside the braces it is declared in (slide 10). See [Four review programs: block scope, hoisting and the event queue](#/comp4537-l3/review-predicts).
hoisting: The JavaScript engine treats var declarations as if they were declared at the top of the function or script, so reading one early prints undefined (slide 13). See [Four review programs: block scope, hoisting and the event queue](#/comp4537-l3/review-predicts).
event queue: Where a setTimeout callback waits until the script has finished, so 1, 3, 2 prints even with 0 ms (slide 16). See [Four review programs: block scope, hoisting and the event queue](#/comp4537-l3/review-predicts).
monolithic: The architecture of small web applications: one web server runs server-side script and returns rendered HTML pages (slide 20). See [Why API servers exist: the online movie store](#/comp4537-l3/why-apis).
screen scraping|HTML scraping: Extracting the data you need (titles, actor names, dates) from inside a page's HTML (slide 23). See [Why API servers exist: the online movie store](#/comp4537-l3/why-apis).
web server: The service for browsers and users; returns HTML pages, which can change any time the site is updated (slide 25). See [Why API servers exist: the online movie store](#/comp4537-l3/why-apis).
API server: The service for data consumer applications; returns JSON/XML and does not change what its URL returns (slide 25). See [Why API servers exist: the online movie store](#/comp4537-l3/why-apis).
API|Application Programming Interface: A user interface to access partners' data and services; in web development, the way we retrieve information from an online service (slide 28). See [Why API servers exist: the online movie store](#/comp4537-l3/why-apis).
API documentation: The list of URLs and query parameters for making a request, and the kind of response each returns (json, text file, xml) (slide 28). See [Why API servers exist: the online movie store](#/comp4537-l3/why-apis).
headers: The additional details provided for communication between client and server, such as API-key on a request and content-type on a response (slide 31). See [Headers, data, endpoint and HTTP method](#/comp4537-l3/anatomy-of-a-web-api).
API key|API-key: The client's subscription key, so the server knows who is making the request (slide 31). See [Headers, data, endpoint and HTTP method](#/comp4537-l3/anatomy-of-a-web-api).
content-type: The response header naming the type of resource the server sent (slide 31). See [Headers, data, endpoint and HTTP method](#/comp4537-l3/anatomy-of-a-web-api).
body|data|message: The part of a request that contains the info you want to send to the server (slide 31). See [Headers, data, endpoint and HTTP method](#/comp4537-l3/anatomy-of-a-web-api).
endpoint: The URL where the API server is listening (slide 32). See [Headers, data, endpoint and HTTP method](#/comp4537-l3/anatomy-of-a-web-api).
HTTP method: Determines the method of communication between client and server: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE (slide 32). See [Headers, data, endpoint and HTTP method](#/comp4537-l3/anatomy-of-a-web-api).
GET: Gets a resource from the server; its query string is sent in the URL (slides 32, 34). See [GET vs POST, and trying an API with Postman](#/comp4537-l3/get-vs-post).
POST: Creates a resource on the server; its data is stored in the request body, not the URL (slides 32, 36). See [GET vs POST, and trying an API with Postman](#/comp4537-l3/get-vs-post).
PUT: Updates an existing resource on the server (slide 32). See [Headers, data, endpoint and HTTP method](#/comp4537-l3/anatomy-of-a-web-api).
DELETE: Deletes an existing resource from the server (slide 32). See [Headers, data, endpoint and HTTP method](#/comp4537-l3/anatomy-of-a-web-api).
query string: The name/value (key/value) pairs after the ? in a GET request's URL, such as name1=value1&name2=value2 (slide 34). See [GET vs POST, and trying an API with Postman](#/comp4537-l3/get-vs-post).
Postman: A tool to test and try an API by setting the method, URL, headers and body and reading the response (slide 40). See [GET vs POST, and trying an API with Postman](#/comp4537-l3/get-vs-post).
REST|RESTful: Representational State Transfer, an architectural style, a set of constraints for API communication between systems, not an architectural pattern (slides 45, 48). See [REST's five constraints and the microservice gateway](#/comp4537-l3/rest-principles).
microservice: A small, independent, lightweight service that does a single task; microservices communicate via RESTful API calls (slides 45, 46). See [REST's five constraints and the microservice gateway](#/comp4537-l3/rest-principles).
API gateway: The single entry point every request goes through; responsible for routing, authentication and auditing (slide 47). See [REST's five constraints and the microservice gateway](#/comp4537-l3/rest-principles).
client-server: REST constraint: the client handles the user interface, the server manages data and business logic (slide 50). See [REST's five constraints and the microservice gateway](#/comp4537-l3/rest-principles).
stateless: REST constraint: each request contains all the info needed; the server doesn't store session state (slide 50). See [REST's five constraints and the microservice gateway](#/comp4537-l3/rest-principles).
cacheable: REST constraint: the server defines whether a response can be cached, via headers like Cache-Control, ETag, Expires (slide 50). See [REST's five constraints and the microservice gateway](#/comp4537-l3/rest-principles).
uniform interface: REST's core constraint: resources identified by unique URLs, manipulated through JSON/XML representations, self-descriptive messages, and HATEOAS (slide 51). See [REST's five constraints and the microservice gateway](#/comp4537-l3/rest-principles).
HATEOAS|Hypermedia as the Engine of Appl: Responses include links for discoverability, such as links to close, comment on or assign an issue (slide 51). See [REST's five constraints and the microservice gateway](#/comp4537-l3/rest-principles).
layered system: REST constraint: the system can have layers (client, proxy, gateway, server) and clients don't know whether they reach the origin server or an intermediary (slide 52). See [REST's five constraints and the microservice gateway](#/comp4537-l3/rest-principles).
code-on-demand: The sixth item on the benefits slide: the server delivers JavaScript for the web app to run, for extensibility (slide 53). See [REST's five constraints and the microservice gateway](#/comp4537-l3/rest-principles).
